 Millions of Social Security payments hitting accounts ahead of schedule: Here’s why
 Updated: Oct. 30, 2026, 2:33 p.m. 
 | Published: Oct. 30, 2026, 6:00 a.m. 
 SSI payments go to more than 7.1 million low-income Americans and those with disabilities. Social Security Administration 
 Set as Google Preferred Source 
 By Leada Gore | lgore@al.com 
 The Social Security Administration is sending millions of payments today, two days ahead of the regular schedule.
 Supplementary Security Income (SSI) payments are hitting account today (Friday, Oct. 30). The change comes due to the regular payment date, Nov. 1, falling on a Sunday. SSI payment dates change when the regular schedule falls on a weekend.
 This means SSI recipients will get two October payments and none in November.
 There are a variety of payment changes in November. Here’s what you need to know: 
 Traditional Social Security comes a day early
 In every other month in 2026, traditional Social Security is paid on a set schedule: people born from the 1st – 10th are paid on the second Wednesday of the month; people born 11th – 20th are paid on the third Wednesday; and people born 21st – 31st are paid on the fourth Wednesday. 
 There’s a change in November, however.
 This year, Veterans Day falls on Wednesday, Nov. 11, the second Wednesday of the month. Because of the federal holiday, millions of Social Security recipients will get their benefits a day earlier, on Tuesday, Nov. 10.
 It’s the only traditional Social Security payment date change in the year.
 Any other changes?
 No. Payments for the rest of the month will fall on their regular dates.
 How many people receive Social Security?
 More than 56 million retirees, dependents and disabled workers receive Social Security benefits. The average monthly benefit for retired workers is $2,084.
 December SSI changes
 Two SSI payments will be issued in December as well. The first will come Tuesday, Dec. 1 and the second on Thursday, Dec. 31. No payment will be issued on New Year’s Day, Friday, Jan. 1, 2027.
 What is SSI?
 More than 7 million people in the U.S. receive benefits through Supplemental Security Income. Payments average about $740 a month and go to low-income senior citizens, people with disabilities and the blind.
 What about people who get Social Security and SSI?
 A separate schedule applies to people who began receiving Social Security before May 1997 or who receive both Social Security and SSI. SSI is issued on the first of each month – if the date doesn’t fall on a holiday or weekend – and Social Security is paid on the third.
 Payment schedule for remainder of 2026:
 Here are SSI and Social Security payment dates for the remainder of 2026:
 October
 Friday, Oct. 30 – SSI payment made early since Nov. 1 falls on a Sunday 
 November
 Tuesday, Nov 3 - Social Security for people who began receiving benefits before May 1997 or are receiving both Social Security and SSI 
 Tuesday, Nov 10 - Social Security for people with birthdates 1st -10th. Paid a day early since Nov. 11 is Veterans Day, a federal holiday. 
 Wednesday, Nov. 18 - Social Security for people with birthdates 11th -20th 
 Wednesday, Nov. 25 - Social Security for people with birthdates 21st -31st 
 December
 Tuesday, Dec. 1 – SSI payments 
 Thursday, Dec. 3 - Social Security for people who began receiving benefits before May 1997 or are receiving both Social Security and SSI 
 Wednesday, Dec. 9 – Social Security for people with birthdates 1st -10th 
 Wednesday, Dec. 16 - Social Security for people with birthdates 11th -20th 
 Wednesday, Dec. 23 - Social Security for people with birthdates 21st -31st 
 Thursday, Dec. 31 – SSI payments for January 2027 since Jan. 1 is the New Year’s federal holiday

 Changes for 2027
 Retirees, survivors and disability recipients, as well as those who receive Supplemental Security Income, will get a 3.6% cost of living adjustment (COLA) in 2027. The figure is the highest in four years.
 The average Social Security check will increase by about $75 a month in 2027. SSI recipients will see an average increase of $59.
